Name the frameworks, papers, and products that ship this (MemGPT/Letta context p
branches.answer:
FINDINGS:
1. MemGPT/Letta: lets an LLM manage a virtual “memory hierarchy” using a persistent store and self-directed retrieval, so the orchestrator sees only the current page (context window) while older data resides in external storage. Buys extension of effective context length without architectural changes. Failure mode: retrieval choice errors discard critical state; delays from paging.
2. Chain-of-Agents (paper, e.g. Google Research 2024): splits a long document across multiple LLM agents, each reading a chunk and inheriting a running summary, the final agent producing a condensed “verdict” for the orchestrator. Buys language-aware summarisation that preserves cross-chunk signals better than simple map-reduce. Failure mode: cumulative error amplification; loss of granular detail necessary for precise reasoning.
3. LLM MapReduce (LangChain, LangGraph, papers): maps parallel LLM calls over document chunks to extract partial answers, then reduces them into a single verdict. Buys horizontal scale and fast processing. Failure mode: reductive fusion loses interactions between chunks; irrelevant fragments can swamp the reducer.
4. Anthropic multi-agent research (e.g. Debate, Constitutional AI critiques): uses one agent to generate content and another to judge, with the judge (or orchestrator) receiving only the arguments, not the full context. Buys oversight under limited attention budget. Failure mode: unfaithful summaries from debate agents may mislead the judge.
5. OpenAI Deep Research (product, 2025): browses the web, takes notes, and synthesises a report; the orchestrator (user) sees only the final referenced report. Buys exhaustive source integration without operator context overflow. Failure mode: hallucinated citations; misinterpretation of source material; nested retrieval misses crucial counter-evidence.
6. Cognition Devin (product): maintains a single-context orchestrator that uses a persistent shell, browser, and editor, reading only tool output summaries (verdicts) to decide next actions. Buys a coherent, replayable developer trace. Failure mode: orchestrator loses the thick texture of raw outputs; long-term plan drift.
7. LangGraph supervisor/map-reduce patterns: orchestrate between specialist agents, with a supervisor seeing only condensed agent responses, while agents execute tool calls or sub-processing. Buys modularity and controllable flow. Failure mode: supervisor can become a bottleneck if verdicts are ambiguous.
8. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation; common product stacking): stores documents in a vector database, retrieves relevant chunks, and feeds only those chunks (plus possibly a summarisation step) to the orchestrator LLM. Buys enormous knowledge bases with fixed context. Failure mode: retrieval misses the right chunks; no global view of the document set.
9. Bitemporal store (databases like Datomic, XTDB, or homegrown): records both valid time and transaction time, enabling queries like “what did the system believe as of date D.” When coupled with context-leverage, it gives the orchestrator a time-aware snapshot of past state without loading full history. Buys auditability, reproducibility, and multi ...-temporal reasoning.  
REASONING: I scanned my training data for systems where an orchestrator consumes only summary verdicts while fan-out workers (agents, scripts, or stores) do the raw reading. I excluded systems where the orchestrator directly ingests primary evidence—those are not context-leverage patterns. Once I had a catalogue, I prioritised steal-worthiness for a 3-seat fleet with a bitemporal store by asking: what gives the smallest, most composable kernel of “verdict-based delegation” that the store can time-version. I ruled out entire heavy products (OpenAI Deep Research, Cognition Devin) because they embed too much undifferentiated machinery. I also set aside pure map-­reduce, because the store already gives you snapshot-­able aggregation; you need a retrieval- and summary-­fusion core that honours temporal dimensions. That left MemGPT-style paging (teaches a single seat to treat the store as an external memory layer) and the Chain-of-Agents summary-merge (teaches two seats to produce a verdict that preserves cross-­context structure). Together they form the minimal loop: Seat A pages out old context to the store; Seats B and C summarise overlapping segments and fuse them, writing both the verdict and the (valid time, transaction time) provenance. The bitemporal store then makes every retrieval “as-of” auditable, which is the missing piece in every other listed pattern.  
CHECK: The cheapest challenge would be to feed the fleet a deliberately ambiguous two-­part legal document where the critical link spans exactly the cut between two chunks; if the bitemporal store can retrieve the bridging link only by changing the “as-of” time, but the seat doing the paging has already frozen its retrieval window, the fleet would still miss it. That would expose a mismatch between temporal-paging policy and the fuzzy boundaries that Chain-of-Agents fusion can smooth over—proving the combination is less robust than a plain long-­context model on that specific rupture.  
BLIND: This analysis cannot see emergent side-­effects from the interplay of paging granularity and the actual RLHF tuning of the fleet models, nor how a human supervisor’s intermittent intervention would alter the optimal “steal” order. It also assumes a pure text-­only domain; multimodal embeddings or tool-­use judgements that proxy for raw sensor data might make direct-­ingestion pipelines (i.e., non-­verdict patterns) sneak back in.
